title: Sleep and teenagers: seven short texts
texts: A can of a fizzy drink full of stimulants, or a strong coffee at four in the afternoon, may seem harmless, yet caffeine stays in the blood for many hours. It does not create new strength; it merely hides tiredness for a while, and the bill arrives later in the form of restless nights. Exhausted students then reach for more of the same, so a small habit turns into a vicious circle.

During the teenage years the brain releases the hormone that makes us drowsy about two hours later than it did in childhood. As a result, a fifteen-year-old who lies awake at ten in the evening is not being difficult; the body simply has not received its signal yet. When darkness falls, adults begin to feel heavy-eyed while their children are still alert, and the pattern only gradually reverses in early adulthood.

While we rest, the brain is far from idle. During the deepest stages of sleep it sorts the information collected during the day, keeping what seems important and discarding the rest; later, in the phase when dreams appear, it links new facts with older ones. That is why a student who revises until dawn often remembers less in the exam than one who goes to bed at a reasonable hour, even on the weekend before a test.

Everyone knows that a poor night makes people yawn, but the consequences go further. Studies link short sleep with irritability, frequent colds and a lack of energy for sport, and drivers who are short of rest cause more accidents. Over months, the lack of rest may even affect mood, making ordinary problems seem much heavier than they are.

Many teenagers stay up late on Friday and Saturday and sleep until noon, hoping to repay the debt of the week. Unfortunately this habit moves the body clock further back, so that on Monday morning it feels as if the family has flown across several time zones overnight. Doctors advise getting up at roughly the same hour every day, perhaps allowing one extra hour, which keeps the rhythm steady.

Many teenagers check their phones until the last minute before they close their eyes. The bright displays of phones and tablets send the brain a confusing message that it is still afternoon, so the usual drowsiness is delayed by half an hour or more. Researchers also note that exciting messages and videos keep the mind busy long after the lights are off. A simple rule, leaving devices outside the bedroom, is surprisingly effective.

Some schools have experimented with moving the first lesson from eight o'clock to nearly nine. The results were encouraging: fewer pupils arrived late, more of them stayed awake in class and marks improved slightly. Teachers admitted that the change caused practical headaches, from bus timetables to after-school clubs, yet few wanted to return to the old arrangement. The experiment suggests that the timetable, not the teenager, may sometimes be the problem.
discuss: How many hours do you sleep on school days? What stops you from sleeping more?
Should schools start later in the morning? Give arguments for and against.
What rules would you set for screens before bedtime?
